The board has asked us to have a humanitarian session at each board because children affected by climate hazard and/or affected by armed conflict continue to have the highest level of deprivation and rights violations. Nearly half of the world's children, or 1.1 billion children, are now exposed to at least three overlapping climate hazards. One in five children globally are living in conflict zones. Nearly half, approximately 50% of all under five child deaths globally occur in fragile and conflict affected settings. In the week when many children are returning to classrooms for a new academic year, it's important to note that 258 million children globally have had their education disrupted by conflicts, climate shocks, and forced displacement. For the third year running, we have recorded the highest number of grave violations against children that have ever been recorded since the creation of the Children Affected by Armed Conflict agenda. The latest trends indicate that children continue to be killed and maimed at staggering levels, as mentioned by Ukraine, Iran, and other delegations during this Board. In 2025, almost 70% of child casualties were caused by explosive weapons in populated areas. Children should not be dying while in their homes, shopping at a mall, or attending school. In addition to physical and psychosocial harm, these weapons destroy schools, hospitals, water systems, power networks, and other civilian infrastructure essential for children's survival and recovery. They leave behind unexploded ordnance that can continue to kill and maim children after hostilities have ended. The UN will continue to do its part to monitor and report these violations. Turning to the subject of this year's oral update on humanitarian action, localization. Localization continues to be one of the key elements of our work and sits at the center of UNICEF's engagement to operationalize and accelerate the humanitarian reset. UNICEF has made critical advances in our localization approach, including consistently meeting grand bargain targets on funding allocated to local organizations, as well as context-specific examples of good localization practices, from supporting the health system backed by local NGOs to respond to the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, to supporting government ownership of the humanitarian response in Iraq through direct engagement with local authorities. Taking stock of a decade of localization in practice, we have laid a solid foundation for more locally led humanitarian action. And while these efforts are not new, they take on new urgency under the humanitarian reset. With crises continuing to expand and grow globally, and with shrinking resources, we must shift from incremental, contextualized improvements to localization to more ambitious and system-wide change geared towards ensuring local and national actors are the first line of response and lead the delivery of substantial and significant humanitarian results at scale. UNICEF has made the case that localization needs to include work with national and local authorities and support to social service delivery systems so that humanitarian responses can be sustainable and we don't create and perpetuate parallel systems. In some parts of Africa, where conflict and displacement, climate-related shocks, food insecurity, disease outbreaks, and other emergencies continue to place significant pressure on communities and national systems, national and local actors are not only the first to respond, they remain present long after international attention has moved elsewhere. The humanitarian reset presents an important opportunity to rethink not only how humanitarian assistance is delivered, but also who leads, who makes decisions, and who has the resources to respond. We note with interest the experience of many African countries and the efforts made to strengthen national leadership and progressively transition critical humanitarian functions towards national and local actors. These experiences offer valuable lessons on the importance of shifting leadership, decision-making capacity, and resources closer to the people affected by crises, while ensuring that National actors are supported to play a meaningful role in determining priorities, designing programs, implementing responses, and assessing results. We encourage UNICEF to build on this experience by continuing to invest in and strengthen national systems and institutions. We also believe that greater national and local leadership should be matched with the necessary resources, capacities, and appropriate sharing of responsibilities and risks to ensure that those taking on greater responsibilities are properly supported to deliver effectively. We value the important role of regional and subregional organizations in preparedness, early warning, cross-border coordination, and the sharing of technical expertise. The group encourages UNICEF to look more closely at the quality of partnerships and the extent to which decision-making and leadership are being localized. We should therefore welcome a more clear evaluation of the localization shift, including on what has changed in practice, what barriers remain, and whether national and local actors have the necessary resources, capacities, and space to take on and sustain leadership. Mr. President, for the Africa Group, localization is about recognizing the knowledge, leadership, and resilience that already exists within communities and national institutions, and ensuring that international assistance strengthens rather than substitutes for these capacities. We therefore encourage UNICEF to continue this important work in close consultation with Member States, national and local actors, regional organizations and affected communities. The success of the humanitarian reset should ultimately be measured not only by the resources mobilized, but by whether it enables more effective, locally led and sustainable action that protects children and leaves stronger national systems behind. I thank you.

First, needs cannot be measured by caseload alone. The RESET and its prioritization frameworks were designed largely around large-scale conflict settings. In small island developing states, the caseload is small. The distances are immense, and the cost of reaching a single child on an outer island is high. On behalf of the delegation of the Executive Board, led by His Excellency Ambassador Rain Kamasar, I'm pleased to present a brief summary for our field trip to Maldives and Sri Lanka undertaken from May 31st to June 4th, 2026. The visit gave Executive Board members an opportunity to engage directly with governments, communities, children and young people, civil society, development partners and UNICEF staff. It provided valuable first-hand perspectives on both progress achieved and challenges that remain for children, adolescents and women. In Maldives, we saw important gains in child survival, maternal health, immunization, education, and access to basic services. At the same time, the visit highlighted emerging challenges for adolescents. Educational transition is a particular concern, with fewer than half of the students continuing to lower to upper secondary education. boys, children in remote islands, and those facing socioeconomic disadvantage encounter particular barriers. We also heard concerns about young people who are neither in education, employment, nor training. This underscored the need to connect education with skills, employment, mental health, and social protection, while giving young people meaningful opportunities to participate in decisions affecting their futures. Child protection, violence prevention, and juvenile justice were also very important areas of discussion with strong emphasis on prevention, early intervention, family support, and community-based approaches. The realities of being a small island developing state were evident throughout the visit. Geographic dispersion and climate vulnerability make equitable service delivery more difficult, while young people themselves demonstrated a strong awareness of climate risks. We also heard concerns regarding UNICEF's planned transition to a multi-country office arrangement with Sri Lanka. Government counterparts stressed the importance of maintaining UNICEF's responsiveness, technical capacity and presence in Maldives. These concerns should remain central to the transition process. In Sri Lanka, we witnessed significant achievements in child survival, health and education, alongside persistent inequalities and pressures associated with economic recovery, climate change and social vulnerability. child protection was a central theme. We saw the potential of family reintegration approaches that combine psychosocial support, improved living conditions, and livelihood assistance to prevent children from remaining in institutional care. Nutrition remains an important challenge among vulnerable communities, while Sri Lanka's strong primary health care system provides an important foundation for integrated maternal child health and nutrition services. In education, high enrollment does not always translate into equitable learning outcomes. Foundational learning, preschool access, the digital divide, violence in schools, and climate anxiety among young people remain important concerns. One particularly powerful message came from young climate advocates. Young people do not want simply to be consulted. They want meaningful opportunities to influence decisions affecting their future. We were also struck by the repeated emphasis on Sri Lanka resilience. While recognizing the remarkable resilience of communities, we felt it important that resilience should not become a substitute for addressing the vulnerabilities and repeated shocks that communities are being asked to absorb. Across both countries, the visit reinforced the value of UNICEF as more than a program implementer. Its greatest contribution can be seen as a partner to governments in strengthening national systems, generating evidence, convening stakeholders, supporting policy, and translating national priorities into sustainable results for the children. The visit also reminded us that resources alone do not guarantee results. timely implementation, effective expenditure, and removing bottlenecks are equally important. This raises an important question for UNICEF and the Board. How do we ensure that available resources, technical assistance, and partnerships translate into tangible and lasting improvement in children's lives? In conclusion, the visit demonstrated that as countries progress, the challenges facing children evolve. The focus must move beyond survival and access towards quality, equity, protection, participation, well-being, skills, and successful transition into adulthood. Our appreciation goes to the governments of Maldives and Sri Lanka, the children and young people who shared their experiences, civil society and development partners, and the entire UNICEF country teams and staff who made the visit possible. I thank you.
